response: The section details the systematic process for building, filtering, and categorizing the literature corpora used in the survey, emphasizing coverage, transparency, volume management, and reproducibility. Figure 4 shows three corpora—Main (81.2 % of 1,263 publications), Implications (9.9 %) and Further (8.9 %)—and outlines the automated acquisition pipeline, filtering strategies, post‑processing steps, and selection criteria for each set.

The authors built a modular Python pipeline (Fig. 5) to automate literature acquisition while limiting manual work to two refinement steps. Users supply one or more Academic Search Query Syntax (ASQS) queries, a date range, target databases (arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus, Semantic Scholar), a retrieval preference (latest vs. most relevant), and per‑query result caps (e.g., 100). The system translates each ASQS query to each database’s syntax, runs all DB‑query permutations, merges returned metadata, and removes duplicates using identifiers such as DOIs. Missing metadata are fetched from auxiliary APIs (Semantic Scholar, arXiv, Crossref) and validated (e.g., title‑abstract consistency); articles with insufficient or erroneous data are excluded, followed by a second duplicate pass. Validated records are saved as JSON/YAML (optionally PDF) with full citation details, and comprehensive retrieval reports are auto‑generated (overall queries, time span, database selection, result counts, timestamps; per‑DB‑query details). An on‑demand GPT‑4o filter scores semantic relevance, returning binary labels, scores ∈[0,1], and brief justifications; filters can be applied sequentially with stricter criteria. A separate GPT‑4o Query Proposal component suggests initial queries based on ASQS definitions and user intent. Final corpora were further refined manually (reference enrichment, hand‑searches, extra filters) to ensure quality and completeness.

Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) extend the concept of foundation models (FMs) from language and vision to robotics, aiming for highly adaptable, data‑driven systems that can be efficiently repurposed across tasks, environments, and hardware with minimal engineering. Like large language models, RFMs are trained on massive, heterogeneous datasets using self‑supervised methods, which can give rise to emergent behaviours that exceed their explicit training objectives. However, robotics introduces closed‑loop, high‑dimensional decision making where actions continuously reshape sensory inputs, and robot platforms vary widely in embodiment and context, demanding models that are task‑agnostic, cross‑embodiment, and open‑ended.

Definitions differ: some authors separate “single‑purpose” RFMs (e.g., perception‑only) from “general‑purpose” RFMs that span perception, planning, control, and even non‑robotic tasks. The survey argues that true RFMs must integrate perception with actionable outputs (control, trajectories, plans). Vision‑Language‑Action models (VLAs) are treated as a distinct sub‑category; they fuse language and vision into a common token format, enabling end‑to‑end training and human‑like instructability, but RFMs are not limited to low‑level actions and may also produce high‑level plans.

The core criteria for an RFM are: (1) multi‑modality—ingestion of proprioceptive, exteroceptive, and natural‑language signals; (2) output flexibility—generation of actions, plans, or trajectories suitable for diverse robots; (3) adaptability—ability to generalise or fine‑tune to new tasks, settings, or embodiments with little manual effort. Sub‑taxonomies include RFMs for control (direct low‑level commands), RFMs for planning (high‑level reasoning and task decomposition), and integrated RFMs that combine both. Even models lacking language inputs, such as vision‑action systems, qualify if they support multi‑purpose adaptation.

Specialised RFMs target domains like manipulation, locomotion, aerial, underwater, or mobile‑manipulation, often reflecting predefined action spaces or fine‑tuning data. Manipulation is highlighted as especially relevant for industrial use, underpinning assembly, pick‑and‑place, and dexterous handling. Ultimately, a model is considered an RFM only when it demonstrates cross‑task or cross‑embodiment adaptability, multimodal integration, and flexible output generation; otherwise it is classified as a narrow or specialised approach.

The introduction frames the shift in industrial robotics from tightly engineered, static automation toward flexible, collaborative systems, especially cobots that must be commissioned quickly, redeployed across changing processes, and operate safely near humans. While modern cobots retain high precision and low power, their practical value is now limited more by the availability of robust, adaptive control methods than by actuation capabilities. This motivates a focus on learning‑based robot intelligence that can handle variability in tasks, environments, sensing, and actuation while meeting industrial constraints such as safety, reliability, low latency and cost‑effective integration.

Recent advances in large‑scale learning have produced Foundation Models (FMs) that transfer knowledge across tasks, giving rise to Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) intended to provide generalist competence for embodied decision‑making. The survey concentrates on RFMs that generate low‑level actions for direct actuation, because this interface is most tightly coupled to industrial constraints (latency, safety gating, hardware‑specific action spaces). Various model families—diffusion‑based, dreaming‑based, dual‑system designs—are acknowledged, but architectural taxonomy is omitted in favor of an industrial lens that links methodological progress to deployment feasibility.

A hierarchical categorisation of robotic control methods is proposed: (1) predefined/rule‑based, (2) reactive/parametrised, (3) specialised/narrow, (4) foundational (pre‑trained, fine‑tunable), and (5) generalist (zero‑shot, online adaptation). The trajectory moves from rigid, task‑specific automation toward instruction‑driven, adaptable operation with reduced commissioning effort. The emergence of RFMs marks the transition from specialised to foundational control, yet true generalist capability—robust online adaptation, dependable instruction following, safe operation under uncertainty—remains unmet for industrial deployment.

Publication trends show a sharp rise in RFMs and related work, especially in 2025, risking fragmentation and overstated claims without systematic industrial evaluation. Existing surveys lack a structured, implication‑grounded assessment of deployment readiness. Consequently, the paper outlines a review methodology, situates RFMs within the broader control landscape, and develops an industrial implication framework (Section 7) comprising eleven viewpoints and a 149‑item criteria catalogue. Applying this framework to manipulation‑capable RFMs (Section 8) reveals that, despite benchmark progress, industrial maturity is limited and uneven: current models typically address only a few enabling dimensions rather than providing integrated coverage of the critical requirements for real‑world factories. The authors aim to shift discourse from isolated benchmark successes to a traceable, industrial‑focused evaluation of what constitutes a credible, deployable RFM.

The RFM‑related corpus was built to cover all major research directions on robotic foundation models (RFMs) and adjacent topics such as training protocols, extensions, applications, safety and robustness. Two large‑scale retrievals were run with an identical Python pipeline (Section 3.1) on 11 extensive ASQS queries across arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus and SemanticScholar, limited to 400 results per database (max 22 000). Search 1 (4 July 2025) yielded 10 728 entries (5 035 unique); Search 2 (30 Oct 2025) returned 12 027 entries (4 999 unique). After merging and a conservative duplicate‑removal step, 6 497 unique articles remained. A coarse LLM filter removed non‑robotics papers, retaining 4 834; a stricter LLM filter for RFM relevance left 1 408 articles, which were manually inspected with no false negatives found. Final manual curation produced 1 025 highly relevant works, split into 341 control/integrated RFMs (324 manipulation‑focused, 17 other domains), 321 related works, 231 high‑level LLM‑based or narrow models, 77 data/benchmark papers, and 55 surveys (24 general AI, 31 including RFMs, 11 RFMs‑specific). This set underpins all subsequent analyses.

The authors built an industrial‑implication corpus using the modular literature pipeline (Sec 3.1). Seven broad ASQS queries (Table B3) searched arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus and Semantic Scholar for 2015‑Jul 2025, retrieving up to 1,750 papers. After deduplication (892 unique) and an LLM relevance filter, 296 articles remained; the 125 highest‑scored (≥0.9) were manually reviewed. These core papers were iteratively synthesized, clustered and mapped to industrial implications for robotic systems, detailed in Sec 7.

source_label: Section: 5 Rise of Cobots in Industry
response: Recent RFMs are mainly shown with cobots in lab, tabletop or kitchen contexts, limiting perceived industrial relevance. To assess broader impact, the section first reviews how industrial robotics has evolved toward collaborative systems, framing cobot growth as part of this transition. This contextual background is needed before evaluating cobot‑driven RFM advances.

The authors surveyed 55 recent review articles and classified them by inclusion of robot‑foundation models (+RFMs), general embodied AI (GEA), and explicit industrial focus (IND). Only 11 papers (20 % of the corpus) target RFMs, and all of these concentrate on vision‑language agents (VLAs); none address industrial applications. Two surveys mention RFMs outside the VLA sub‑category—Zhou et al. on language‑conditioned manipulation and Hu et al. on the broader RFM paradigm—but they still lack an industrial perspective. Industrial‑oriented reviews are even scarcer: just two of the 55 (3.6 %) discuss industrial use cases, and both limit themselves to high‑level vision‑language models for human‑robot collaboration in smart manufacturing, without examining RFMs or their control‑oriented variants. The tables summarising the RFM‑focused and industrial‑focused surveys could not be reliably reconstructed, so detailed entries are omitted. This analysis reveals a pronounced gap: no existing survey links RFMs—especially vision‑action or integrated control models—to industrial requirements, nor evaluates how industrial maturity should influence RFM design. The present work therefore positions itself to fill this void by providing a taxonomy, a comprehensive overview of the RFM landscape, and an analysis of the attributes demanded by industrial scenarios, a perspective absent from current literature.

source_label: Section: 5.1 Landscape of Industrial Robotics: Tradition & Transformation
response: Industrial robots are defined as automatically controlled, reprogrammable manipulators with three‑plus axes, built on an incomplete‑machine architecture that requires external tooling (e.g., grippers, welders). Their complex kinematic chains give high speed, large payloads and accuracy, so they are deployed in isolated, hazardous spaces for repetitive heavy‑duty tasks. Six traditional configurations—Delta (parallel PPP), Cartesian (serial PPP), Cylindrical (RPP), SCARA (RRP), Spherical (RRR/RRP) and Articulated (RRR)—vary in workspace shape and precision, yet all lack intrinsic flexibility, safe direct human‑robot collaboration (HRC) and intuitive programming. Cobots arose to fill this gap: originally passive guides, they now form a sub‑category of articulated robots with lower payloads, reduced speeds, rounded shapes and sensor suites for real‑time contact or human detection. Designed for safe HRC, rapid reconfiguration, and intuitive HRI, cobots target SMEs that need high product variability, small batches, and minimal downtime, shifting the functional ethos from replacing humans to augmenting human capability in shared workspaces.

Cobot deployment still struggles with autonomous handling of complex, cognitive, or dexterous tasks, real‑time hazard detection, continuous safety, and trustworthy HRI/HRC, limiting their industrial use despite benefits for routine or ergonomic work. Integrating RFMs can supply intuitive instruction, multimodal sensing, and advanced reasoning to improve autonomy, adaptation, trust and transparency, but models must be robust beyond controlled labs to meet safety‑critical, variable factory conditions. This creates a feedback loop: cobots expose RFM weaknesses while RFMs can expand cobot capabilities.

Modern cobots, thanks to greater flexibility and safety, have moved beyond labs into diverse real‑world sectors. In manufacturing they handle precision‑critical, adaptable tasks such as assembly, pick‑and‑place, machine tending, quality inspection, palletising, packaging, welding and gluing; examples include UR10e robots at PSA and Fiat Chrysler for door, hood and soft‑top assembly and rivetting. Vision‑enabled cobots inspect dimensions and defects, e.g., UR3s checking automotive touchscreen panels. Integrated with AMRs, they transport components and support just‑in‑time logistics, as seen with MiR200 units in appliance factories. In healthcare they aid patient handling, rehabilitation, medication dispensing and surgical assistance. Agriculture benefits from continuous planting, harvesting and sorting, reducing seasonal labour. Retail and service use cobots for shelf stocking, object retrieval and customer interaction. Military and security employ sensor‑equipped cobots for luggage scanning, hazardous substance detection, bomb disposal, facility inspection, cleaning (e.g., Space Rider orbiter surface cleaning) and border inspection, improving throughput and operator safety.

source_label: Section: 5.3 Drivers of the Industrial Shift Toward Cobots
response: Industrial and commercial sectors are moving from sole reliance on manual labour or traditional robots toward cobots, driven by technological, organisational and economic factors that demand adaptable, user‑friendly automation. Conventional robots excel at high‑volume, repetitive tasks but are costly, complex and hard to reconfigure, limiting SME adoption. Cobots offer flexible design, compact size and intuitive programming, enabling rapid redeployment, reduced integration time and lower expertise needs. They assist humans on repetitive, hazardous work, improve safety, and allow direct human‑robot collaboration through sensors, force‑torque monitoring and adaptive behaviour, cutting barrier costs. Research and practice reflect this shift: cobot‑focused publications grew >5‑fold in a decade, and global installations rose from 11 000 in 2017 to 55 000 in 2022, while their share of total industrial robots increased. Advances in vision and adaptive control further align cobots with Industry 4.0 goals of smart, reconfigurable factories.

The section outlines hardware prerequisites for deploying RFMs with cobots, noting that current cobots lack autonomous cognitive abilities that RFMs can fill. It surveys cobot reach, payload, accuracy, power use, and perception/manipulation hardware, then details industrial edge computing platforms for real‑time inference and the sensing/manipulation components needed for practical, efficient integration.

The survey by Taesi et al. synthesises data from 180 articulated cobot models, showing a mean of 6.09 DOFs and a median payload of 5.5 kg (mean 8.56 kg). Typical reach is about 910 mm (mean 970 mm) and positioning accuracy averages 0.09 mm (median 0.05 mm), though outliers such as the Comau Aura reach 2790 mm and lift 170 kg, inflating the means. For cobots handling 0.5–20 kg payloads (n = 63), peak TCP speed ranges 0.2–6 m/s, usually 1.1–1.68 m/s, while power consumption stays low at 0.25–0.31 kW (mean 0.31 kW, max 0.9 kW). This contrasts with conventional industrial robots that average ~3 kW and peak at 12–15 kW. The modest energy demand supports deployment in power‑constrained settings, mobile or battery‑powered platforms, and emphasizes the need for efficient, low‑latency models within cobot control systems.

Sensors are the primary means for cobot perception and self‑monitoring, supporting HRC, HRI, navigation, manipulation and real‑time task execution. Typical suites combine visual (RGB, depth, CCD), range (LiDAR, RADAR, sonar, TOF, laser), dynamics (IMU, gyroscope, force/torque, tactile, pressure), position/identification (encoders, RFID, GPS, odometry) and specialised (acoustic, thermal) modalities. Fusion—e.g., vision with proximity or force feedback—enhances robustness, safety and compliance, especially for precise handling or contact detection. End‑effectors (grippers, suction cups, dual‑stage tools, custom drills/polishers) often embed sensors (force, vision) and are modular, enabling rapid task reconfiguration but requiring equally flexible control algorithms. This hardware diversity expands observation‑action permutations, underscoring the need for multi‑modal, output‑flexible control in real‑world RFMs.

The section outlines how industrial deployment adds constraints—heterogeneous hardware, safety/compliance, reliability, and continuous operation—that differ from labs. It extracts eleven domain‑agnostic industrial implications from the implication corpus, maps them to detailed attributes for pinpointing constraint locations in RFMs and their ecosystem, and compiles a criteria catalogue to evaluate industrial maturity consistently.

Industrial cobotic systems require real‑time AI control, so computation is placed on edge devices that sit close to the robot to keep latency low and network traffic minimal. Fog or cloud alternatives can add scalability but introduce extra infrastructure, networking dependencies and higher latency, which is problematic for time‑critical control. Recent industrial deployments increasingly favor edge computing because compute costs have fallen and networking expenses are reduced.

The review focuses on NVIDIA Jetson devices as a representative edge‑AI portfolio, since their specifications, pricing and performance metrics are publicly documented, enabling reproducible comparisons. Table 6 lists INT8‑precision AI throughput (TOPS), memory, power draw, and derived efficiency ratios for each Jetson model, plus a desktop‑class RTX 5090 for context. Prices reflect single‑unit purchases on a common date; operational cost assumes 24/7 use at $0.25 /kWh.

Key findings: the Orin Nano line offers the lowest purchase price (≈ $229) while delivering high TOPS‑per‑dollar, making it attractive for cost‑sensitive or large‑scale deployments. The entry‑level Xavier NX provides the lowest absolute AI compute (21 TOPS) but its 8 GB variant has the smallest maximum power draw (15 W), suiting energy‑constrained applications. Mid‑tier devices such as the Orin AGX 32 GB balance higher throughput (200 TOPS) with moderate power (40 W) and achieve the best compute‑per‑operational‑cost efficiency. High‑end Thor series and the RTX 5090 reach the greatest throughput (≥ 517 TOPS, 838 TOPS respectively) but consume substantially more power (130 W, 575 W) and incur higher annual energy costs, limiting their use on mobile or battery‑powered robots.

Industrial‑class (IND) variants add features like ECC memory for reliability, which can increase both capital and operational expenses and sometimes reduce raw compute compared with research‑grade models. Overall, the analysis underscores a trade‑off: larger, more capable robotic foundation models must be matched to edge hardware that satisfies both compute performance and energy‑efficiency constraints to remain practical for real‑world industrial deployment.

The authors translate eleven high‑level industrial implications for robot‑focused foundation models (RFMs) into a concrete set of deployment‑relevant attributes. By analysing each implication against 47 consolidated attributes—spanning hardware, sensing, actions, safety, security, adaptability, real‑time performance, compliance, documentation and more—they generate a 11 × 47 matrix (517 implication‑attribute cells) that captures how each industrial concern would manifest in an RFM‑based system. This systematic traversal exposes inter‑dependencies (e.g., safety with perception, real‑time feasibility with interaction) and prevents overlooking requirements that might be hidden under broader headings. The resulting attribute framework serves as an intermediate, traceable representation for the criteria catalogue (Section 7.3) and underpins an assessment framework that evaluates existing RFMs for industrial readiness, while the full matrix is omitted due to size. The table reconstruction is noted as unreliable.

The section surveys 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs, rating each against 149 implication‑grounded criteria (48,276 decisions) to produce overall maturity scores and implication‑wise profiles. It details the scalable evaluation method, validates it with 28 expert judgments, and then highlights top‑performing models, analyzes industrial applicability for the full set and a Top‑50 subset, and uses these findings to define current industrial maturity, pinpoint well‑ and poorly‑addressed implications, and establish a baseline for later synthesis.

source_label: Section: 7.3 Evaluating Industrial Maturity: A Criteria Catalogue
response:
The section translates the eleven industrial implications for robotic foundation models (RFMs) into a concrete assessment tool. Building on 517 implication‑attribute pairs, the authors distilled 149 criteria that span model capabilities, ecosystem requirements, and joint responsibilities. Criteria are grouped as RFM‑centric (e.g., adaptive behavior under observation/action shifts), ecosystem‑centric (e.g., documentation of training data and transfer behavior), or hybrid (e.g., structured signals for persistent logging). Redundancy is intentional: the same concern—such as hot‑swapping—appears under multiple implications with distinct industrial emphases, preserving diagnostic granularity.

Key paradigms reflected in the catalogue include: (1) multi‑hardware support and runtime adaptation to changing observation/action interfaces, supported by recent work on unified action representations and variable‑size spaces; (2) robustness to out‑of‑distribution (OOD) conditions, adversarial attacks, and anomalies, with repeated demands for online detection, confidence signaling, and fallback mechanisms; (3) calibrated uncertainty and confidence reporting to enable safe halting, logging, and escalation; (4) interactive clarification and human‑in‑the‑loop feedback for ambiguous natural‑language commands, leveraging approaches that generate follow‑up questions or allow trajectory adjustments; (5) decoupled supervisory layers for failure detection and recovery, drawing on VLM‑based safety gating and task‑agnostic monitoring; (6) memory, data governance, and documentation, motivated by lightweight memory modules, privacy‑preserving training, and datasets that embed failure cases.

The authors note that most criteria correspond to active research strands rather than absent technologies; the immaturity lies in integrating these pieces into a systematic, auditable, safety‑governed RFM ecosystem. The catalogue thus serves as a living framework to evaluate current RFMs, pinpoint industrial gaps, and guide future research toward credible industrial deployment.

The authors synthesized 125 manually reviewed industrial studies to extract recurring requirements for robotic systems, grouping statements about needs, constraints, and deployment challenges into eleven inter‑dependent implications. No contradictory themes emerged; instead, the same practical issues (e.g., human presence) appear under multiple lenses such as safety, interaction design, robustness, or perception, and the synthesis separates “what” is demanded from “why”.

1. **Adaptability & Flexibility** – Industrial settings are dynamic, with frequent process changes, product variants, and unpredictable events, especially when humans share the workspace. Traditional automation is brittle; robots must re‑configure online, handle environmental variation (lighting, weather, clutter), and support cobot re‑use across tasks, embodiments, and sensor setups without costly re‑programming.

2. **Safety & Compliance** – Safety is a gating factor, particularly for collaborative robots. Systems must prevent injuries, satisfy standards (e.g., ISO 10218, ISO/TS 15066) and certification, and remain safe under human behavioural variability and sensing uncertainty. Overly conservative safety stops can hurt efficiency, motivating safety‑aware reasoning that preserves productivity.

3. **Human‑Robot Interaction & Collaboration (HRI/HRC)** – Future industrial robots are expected to work closely with humans, requiring diverse interaction regimes (coexistence, cooperation, collaboration) and intuitive, multimodal interfaces (speech, natural gestures). Operators need to instruct, supervise, and correct robots directly, and control must be reactive to uncertainty to sustain fluid workflows.

4. **Robustness & Reliability** – Environments are noisy and prone to disturbances, sensor degradation, and OOD inputs. Robust methods must integrate perception, planning, and control under stochastic and adversarial conditions, provide fault awareness, and maintain stable operation despite hardware or cybersecurity threats.

5. **Precision & Accuracy** – High repeatability and quality‑critical execution remain essential. Both actuation and perception must meet stringent accuracy demands, especially for tasks like grasping and positioning, while preserving throughput.

6. **Real‑Time Performance** – Tight latency bounds are required across sensing, decision‑making, communication, and actuation, even on resource‑constrained edge devices. Real‑time planning in dynamic scenes remains an open challenge; smaller models may enable feasible inference.

7. **Cost‑Effectiveness & Integration** – Automation must be economically justified, especially for low‑volume or SME contexts. Solutions should reduce commissioning effort, be easy to integrate into existing factory architectures, and run on cost‑sensitive hardware, given that high‑tier GPUs can exceed the power budget of a median cobot.

8. **Explainability & Trust** – Transparency and interpretability are needed for operator acceptance, especially where failures have severe consequences. Explainable AI, ergonomic interfaces, and visible system status foster trust and safe collaboration.

9. **Sensor Fusion & Perception** – No single modality suffices; multi‑modal sensing (vision, tactile, external sensors) and fusion are required to handle occlusions, lighting changes, and sensor degradation, supporting safe HRC and robust operation.

10. **Standardised Benchmarking & Evaluation** – Reproducible, task‑relevant benchmarks and digital‑twin‑based testing are needed to assess performance, interoperability, and reliability across complex industrial systems.

11. **Data Requirements & Usage** – Industrial domains face data scarcity, costly collection, and simulation‑to‑real gaps. Methods must be data‑efficient (few‑shot, continual learning), handle heterogeneous data, and support transfer under realistic deployment constraints.

These implications frame the bottlenecks that cause laboratory‑grade learning approaches to falter in production, and they guide the subsequent assessment of robotic foundation models for industrial readiness.

The authors evaluated industrial readiness for every manipulation‑capable robot‑learning foundation model (RFM) in their corpus—324 papers out of 341 total—by checking each against a catalogue of 149 implication‑grounded criteria, producing 48 276 criterion‑level decisions. Because manual annotation at this scale was infeasible, they built an automated pipeline that queries a large language model (GPT‑5.1) for each paper‑criterion pair in strict isolation: the model sees only one criterion and one paper (with figures) via a dedicated vector store that is deleted after each decision, preventing any cross‑contamination or leakage. The LLM returns a structured record containing a binary fulfil‑ment judgment, a direct‑statement flag, a confidence score, an evidence‑availability flag, extracted quotes, and a brief rationale. The system is instructed to be conservative, marking a criterion as unfulfilled unless the paper clearly supports it, which yields deliberately cautious maturity estimates.

To validate the pipeline, three papers were independently annotated by experts (two beforehand, one after the LLM run). At the implication level the LLM reproduced expert patterns, showing Gemini Robotics 1.5 markedly more mature than OpenVLA, while π0 remained limited. Across 447 criterion‑level comparisons the LLM achieved 96.6 % accuracy, F1 = 0.762 for the positive class, Cohen’s κ = 0.744, a low false‑positive rate (1.9 %) and a higher false‑negative rate (22.6 %), reflecting the conservative policy. Filtering by the “information‑found” flag did not improve F1, confirming it mainly signals evidence presence rather than correctness. Per‑paper agreement was high for Gemini Robotics 1.5 and OpenVLA but lower for π0, where positives were rare (2.7 %) and small disagreement magnified metric effects. Discrepancies often stemmed from interpretive ambiguity in criteria (e.g., what counts as “few‑shot” adaptation or “mid‑execution feedback”), not outright errors. Some criteria are inherently strict (e.g., guarantees expressed as “always”), leading the LLM to mark them unfulfilled unless near‑perfect performance is claimed.

Overall, the comparison shows the pipeline provides reliable, conservative maturity estimates suitable for corpus‑scale analysis, with minimal over‑claiming and acceptable agreement for implication‑level trends. However, the elevated miss rate and criterion‑level interpretive latitude advise caution when interpreting individual fine‑grained results; the authors therefore focus subsequent analysis on implication‑level patterns rather than isolated criteria.

The authors evaluated 324 robot‑foundation models (RFMs) against an implication‑grounded industrial maturity framework.  The five overall highest‑rated models (Table 11) achieve total scores of only 0.11–0.12, corresponding to roughly one‑tenth of the catalogue criteria satisfied on average.  Gemini Robotics 1.5 attains the top total (0.12) and the strongest score on adaptability/flexibility (I1 = 0.44), the sole value above 0.4 across all RFMs.  All other top models cluster around 0.28–0.33 on I1 and display isolated peaks on a few other implications (e.g., I10 = 0.21 for Collab‑VLA, I11 = 0.27 for GF‑VLA, I4 = 0.21 and I5 = 0.23 for SC‑VLA).  These patterns reflect a common design choice: the best systems do not present a monolithic visuo‑motor policy but combine multiple components that target specific failure modes—structured reasoning, human‑in‑the‑loop guidance, self‑correction, or enhanced perception/data use.  Consequently, their maturity profiles show pronounced peaks on a small subset of implications while remaining low elsewhere (Fig. 10).

Agreement between expert and LLM‑based evaluations was high.  Across 447 implication assessments the overall accuracy was 96.6 % with an F1 of 0.762 and Cohen’s κ = 0.744; false‑positive and false‑negative rates were 1.9 % and 22.6 % respectively (Table 9).  When restricting to cases where information was found, accuracy fell slightly to 95.1 % but κ remained comparable (0.734).  Per‑paper agreement (Table 10) shows that Gemini 1.5, OpenVLA and π0 achieve expert‑positive rates of 12.1 %, 6.0 % and 2.7 % respectively, with Jaccard similarity indices ranging from 0.167 to 0.714, confirming that the LLM pipeline reliably captures the limited industrial relevance present in these works.

A per‑implication ranking (Table 12) reveals that different models dominate different criteria: Collab‑VLA leads on I1 (0.28) and I8 (0.11); GF‑VLA scores highest on I11 (0.27); SC‑VLA attains the top I4 (0.33) and I5 (0.23); HiBer scores highest on I3 (0.11); Sirius‑HiBer peaks on I2 (0.39).  Nevertheless, even the best per‑implication values remain modest; the highest proportional fulfilment observed is 0.44 (Gemini 1.5 on I1), and no model exceeds 0.33 on any other implication.

The authors interpret these findings as evidence of a “ceiling effect”: current RFMs address only narrow subsets of industrial requirements, typically advancing one or two enabling dimensions at a time. Industrial robotics is shifting from isolated automation to collaborative cobot deployments, especially in high‑mix, low‑volume and SME contexts where traditional automation is costly and inflexible. Modern cobots supply safe hardware, suitable payloads and low power draw, yet the core bottleneck remains robust, deployment‑ready intelligence that can adapt to varied tasks, environments and multimodal inputs without heavy engineering effort.  

The review positions robot‑foundation models (RFMs) as a promising solution because they target multi‑task competence, cross‑domain generalisation and low‑effort reconfiguration—areas where classical control and specialised learning fall short. However, cobot constraints—high precision, moderate payload, low median power (0.5‑20 kg class), heterogeneous sensing and modular end‑effectors—demand low‑latency, energy‑aware inference on edge platforms and flexible interfaces that tolerate changing observation and action spaces.  

To capture these realities the authors derived eleven interdependent industrial implications, mapped to 47 deployment‑relevant attributes, yielding a 11 × 47 matrix and a catalogue of 149 concrete criteria spanning model capabilities and ecosystem requirements. Evaluation of 324 RFMs across 48 276 criterion decisions shows that even top models meet only 0.11‑0.12 of the criteria (≈1 in 10), typically excelling in only two or three implications. Current progress isolates individual bottlenecks—adaptability, benchmarking, data usage—while safety/compliance, HRI/HRC, real‑time performance and cost‑effectiveness remain under‑addressed.  

The authors recommend moving toward layered, deployable architectures that integrate planning, memory, verification and safety gating; developing edge‑focused, low‑latency evaluation protocols; and expanding benchmarks to reflect distribution shifts, failure recovery and long‑horizon operation. Closing gaps in safety, real‑time feasibility and integration is essential for RFMs to become reliable, industrial‑grade autonomy.

The industrial applicability catalogue enumerates a comprehensive set of capabilities that a robot‑control system must exhibit to be viable in modern production environments. Adaptability is foregrounded: the system should operate across heterogeneous kinematic structures, sensors and end‑effectors without retraining, and support hot‑swappable hardware that it detects and configures at runtime. Task flexibility requires handling multiple, possibly unseen, task categories, switching between them only on explicit user instruction, while ensuring that any strategic adaptation remains aligned with the commanded goal and triggers feedback or halting if deviation exceeds a confidence threshold. Environmental robustness is demanded through consistent performance under varied lighting, weather, material and clutter conditions, autonomous handling of distractors, continuous online adaptation to faults or sensor degradation, and the ability to select context‑appropriate fallback behaviours without pre‑programmed scripts.

Safety considerations are extensive. The system must comply with relevant industrial standards, integrate with existing safety infrastructure, and provide traceable documentation of safety reasoning. It should emit confidence scores for safety margins before execution, maintain safety rule enforcement after any model adaptation, and perform real‑time safety evaluation that can pre‑emptively halt or replan when risks arise. High‑level planning must incorporate safety confidence, and the system must autonomously reject unsafe operator commands, employ redundant safety mechanisms, and separate safety gating from action execution. Authorized operators alone may override safety, and safety signals must be shareable with other plant systems. Fault detection must span hardware, sensors, environment and internal representations, with reproducible diagnosis, threat monitoring, and autonomous safe‑state recovery. Transparent logging of safety events and explanations of risk assessments are required.

Human‑robot interaction is specified to be multimodal, offering instruction and feedback via speech, text, gestures, images or demonstrations, and providing confidence scores for input recognition. The interface must remain interruptible and continuously responsive, enforce a single active authorized operator, protect operator data, and adapt to individual preferences. The robot should sense human presence, adjust speed and safety margins, and behave as an adaptive teammate, explaining its reasoning on demand. 

Robustness criteria include multi‑level fault detection, reproducible diagnosis, threat detection, automated recovery, graceful degradation, and dynamic modality management to sustain operation despite sensor loss or disturbances. The system must maintain consistent velocity, precision and accuracy (v/P&A) across tasks, log outcomes, output confidence scores, propose alternative performance trade‑offs, and learn from past failures. Real‑time guarantees must hold regardless of task complexity, input dimensionality or hardware degradation, with dynamic resource management that throttles non‑critical functions to preserve core safety and latency. 

Cost‑efficiency demands operation on low‑cost edge hardware, dynamic resource allocation to reduce energy use, and universal integration without retraining. Hot‑swapping, autonomous commissioning, flexible I/O adaptation, and self‑diagnosis with actionable feedback are required. Documentation must be comprehensive, covering supported platforms, integration steps, performance monitoring and cost‑optimisation histories. 

Explainability permeates the design: the system must disclose task feasibility, reasoning behind decisions, influences of environmental factors, and confidence explanations across all modules. Sensor fusion criteria require acceptance of diverse modalities, continuous monitoring for degradation, dynamic prioritisation of inputs, and robust perception that yields confidence scores and modular feature exposure. The paper begins by observing that industrial robotics is shifting from rigid, static automation toward flexible, collaborative cobots that must be commissioned quickly, redeployed across changing processes, and operate safely alongside humans. This transition makes robust adaptive control the primary bottleneck, outweighing actuation challenges. To address this, the authors survey learning‑based robot intelligence with a focus on Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs), which output low‑level actions directly and therefore align closely with industrial constraints such as latency, safety gating, and hardware‑specific action spaces. A hierarchical taxonomy of control approaches is proposed, ranging from predefined rule‑based systems to generalist models capable of zero‑shot and online adaptation, illustrating a move from task‑specific automation to instruction‑driven, adaptable operation.

RFMs are defined as foundation‑model‑style systems for robotics that ingest multimodal data (proprioceptive, exteroceptive, natural‑language) and produce flexible outputs (actions, plans, trajectories) for diverse robots. They must generalise or fine‑tune to new tasks, settings, or embodiments with minimal engineering. Sub‑taxonomies include low‑level control‑oriented models, high‑level planning‑oriented models, and integrated models that combine both; vision‑language‑action models form a related subset, while pure vision‑action systems also qualify if they support multi‑purpose adaptation. An approach is classified as an RFM only when it demonstrably adapts across tasks or embodiments, integrates multiple modalities, and generates flexible outputs; otherwise it remains a narrow or specialised method.

To evaluate the rapidly expanding literature, the authors built a systematic review pipeline. A modular Python system automates literature acquisition across multiple databases (arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus, Semantic Scholar) using user‑supplied Academic Search Query Syntax (ASQS) queries, date ranges, and result caps. The pipeline translates queries, merges metadata, removes duplicates via identifiers, fetches missing fields from auxiliary APIs, validates records, and stores the results as JSON/YAML with optional PDFs. An on‑demand GPT‑4o filter scores semantic relevance, providing binary labels, confidence scores, and brief justifications; filters can be chained for stricter selection. A separate GPT‑4o component suggests initial queries. After automated retrieval, manual refinement (reference enrichment, hand‑searches, extra filters) ensures quality.

Applying this pipeline to RFM‑related literature, the authors executed two large retrievals (July 2025 and October 2025) across eleven ASQS queries, each limited to 400 results per database, yielding up to 22 000 raw entries. After merging, duplicate removal, and coarse LLM filtering to exclude non‑robotics papers, 4 834 entries remained; a stricter filter for RFM relevance left 1 408, which were manually inspected with no false negatives. The final curated set comprises 1 025 highly relevant works, split into 341 control/integrated RFMs (324 focused on manipulation, 17 on other domains), 321 related works, 231 high‑level LLM‑based or narrow models, 77 data/benchmark papers, and 55 surveys. An additional industrial‑implication corpus was built from seven broad ASQS queries covering 2015‑July 2025, resulting in 125 manually reviewed papers that were clustered and mapped to industrial implications. Further auxiliary searches added 113 publications on related hardware, standards, and efficiency issues.

A review of existing surveys reveals a pronounced gap: among 55 recent review articles, only 11 (20 %) address RFMs, all concentrating on vision‑language agents, and none consider industrial applications. Only two surveys (3.6 %) discuss industrial use cases, and both limit themselves to high‑level vision‑language models for human‑robot collaboration, without evaluating control‑oriented RFMs. Consequently, no existing survey links RFMs—especially vision‑action or integrated control models—to industrial requirements, underscoring the need for the present work.

The authors contextualise cobot growth. Traditional industrial robots are high‑speed, high‑payload manipulators with fixed toolings, deployed in isolated hazardous spaces for repetitive heavy‑duty tasks. Cobots, a sub‑category of articulated robots with lower payloads, reduced speeds, rounded shapes, and rich sensor suites, are designed for safe human‑robot collaboration, rapid reconfiguration, and intuitive programming, targeting SMEs that need high product variability and minimal downtime. Modern cobots have moved beyond labs into manufacturing (assembly, pick‑and‑place, machine tending, inspection, welding, gluing, palletising, packaging), healthcare, agriculture, retail, service, military, and security, often integrated with autonomous mobile robots for just‑in‑time logistics. Drivers of this shift include the high cost and inflexibility of traditional robots, the need for adaptable, user‑friendly automation, and the ability of cobots to assist humans on repetitive or hazardous work while reducing integration time and expertise requirements. Publication counts for cobot‑focused research have grown more than fivefold in a decade, and global installations rose from 11 000 in 2017 to 55 000 in 2022, with their share of total industrial robots increasing. Nevertheless, cobots still struggle with autonomous handling of complex, cognitive, or dexterous tasks, real‑time hazard detection, continuous safety, and trustworthy interaction, limiting broader industrial adoption.

Hardware considerations are detailed. A synthesis of 180 articulated cobot models shows a mean of 6.09 DOFs, median payload 5.5 kg (mean 8.56 kg), typical reach around 910 mm (mean 970 mm), and positioning accuracy averaging 0.09 mm. For payloads 0.5–20 kg, peak TCP speeds range 0.2–6 m/s (usually 1.1–1.68 m/s) and power consumption stays low at 0.25–0.31 kW (mean 0.31 kW), contrasting with conventional robots that average ~3 kW and peak at 12–15 kW. Sensor suites combine vision, depth, LiDAR, radar, sonar, TOF, IMU, force/torque, tactile, encoders, RFID, GPS, and specialised modalities; fusion of vision with proximity or force feedback enhances robustness and safety. End‑effectors are modular and often embed sensors, enabling rapid task reconfiguration but demanding flexible control algorithms. Because low latency is critical, computation is placed on edge devices. The review focuses on NVIDIA Jetson platforms, comparing INT8 AI throughput, memory, power draw, and efficiency. The Orin Nano offers the lowest purchase price (~$229) with high TOPS‑per‑dollar, suitable for cost‑sensitive deployments. The Xavier NX provides the smallest power draw (15 W) for energy‑constrained applications. Mid‑tier Orin AGX 32 GB balances higher throughput (200 TOPS) with moderate power (40 W) and achieves the best compute‑per‑operational‑cost efficiency. High‑end Thor series and RTX 5090 deliver the greatest throughput (≥ 517 TOPS) but consume substantially more power (130–575 W) and incur higher annual energy costs, limiting suitability for mobile or battery‑powered robots. Industrial‑class variants add reliability features such as ECC memory, increasing both capital and operational expenses and sometimes reducing raw compute. The analysis highlights a trade‑off: more capable RFMs must be matched to edge hardware that satisfies both performance and energy constraints to remain practical.

The authors map these high‑level implications to 47 concrete attributes, forming an 11 × 47 matrix that captures how each industrial concern would manifest in an RFM‑based system, exposing inter‑dependencies such as safety with perception and real‑time feasibility with interaction. From this matrix, 149 criteria are distilled, grouped as RFM‑centric (e.g., adaptive behaviour under observation/action shifts), ecosystem‑centric (e.g., documentation of training data and transfer behaviour), or hybrid (e.g., structured signals for persistent logging). Redundancy is intentional to preserve diagnostic granularity; the same concern may appear under multiple implications with distinct industrial emphases.

The authors then evaluate 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs against the 149 criteria, generating 48 276 binary decisions. The review examined 324 robot‑foundation models (RFMs) published between 2020 and 2025 and a high‑performing Top‑50 subset to assess how well current research aligns with the practical demands of modern industrial robotics. Eleven inter‑dependent industrial implications (I1–I11) were defined, covering adaptability/flexibility, safety/compliance, human‑robot interaction, real‑time performance, cost‑effectiveness, explainability, robustness, integration, benchmarking, and data governance. Across the full corpus, the dominant research focus was on adaptability (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10), and data usage (I11). Breadth of coverage was modest, with only I1 (0.756), I10 (0.753) and I11 (0.707) reaching a 1‑plus coverage score; depth (average criterion fulfilment, ACC) was uniformly low, below 0.10 for all implications. The Top‑50 models showed improved breadth, attaining a full 1.0 score for several implications (I1, I4, I5, I8, I9, I10, I11) and modest depth gains (e.g., I1 = 0.238). The most frequently cited criteria belonged to the three well‑covered implications. This indicates that while researchers are increasingly aware of industrial constraints, actual implementations fall far short of delivering comprehensive, criterion‑complete solutions, especially for safety, real‑time operation, cost‑effectiveness and human‑robot interaction.

The discussion contextualises these findings within the broader shift from isolated automation toward collaborative cobots, particularly in high‑mix, low‑volume and SME settings where traditional lines are uneconomical. Modern cobots provide safe hardware, modest payloads (0.5–20 kg) and low power draw, but the critical bottleneck is robust, deployment‑ready intelligence that can adapt to varied tasks, environments and multimodal inputs without extensive engineering. RFMs are positioned as a promising avenue because they aim for multi‑task competence, cross‑domain generalisation and low‑effort reconfiguration—areas where classical control and specialised learning struggle. However, cobot constraints also demand low‑latency, energy‑aware inference on edge platforms and flexible interfaces that tolerate changing observation and action spaces.

Quantitatively, the authors evaluated 324 RFMs against 48 276 individual criterion decisions. Even the best models satisfied only about 11–12 % of the criteria (roughly one in ten), typically excelling in just two or three implications. Adaptability, benchmarking and data usage were the only areas where any substantial progress was observed; safety/compliance, HRI/HRC, real‑time performance and cost‑effectiveness remained largely untouched.

Appendix C details the industrial implication catalogue. Adaptability requires operation across heterogeneous kinematics, sensors and end‑effectors without retraining, hot‑swappable hardware detection, and task‑category switching on explicit user instruction, while maintaining strategic goal alignment and halting when confidence falls below a threshold. Safety demands compliance with standards, pre‑execution confidence scores, rule enforcement after model updates, real‑time risk evaluation capable of pre‑emptive halting or replanning, and restricted override rights. Interaction must be multimodal (speech, text, gesture, image, demonstration) with confidence reporting, interruptibility, single‑operator enforcement and adaptive teammate behaviour. Robustness calls for multi‑level fault detection, reproducible diagnosis, automated recovery, graceful degradation, consistent velocity/precision, real‑time guarantees and dynamic resource throttling. Cost‑efficiency targets low‑cost edge hardware, dynamic energy management, hot‑swapping, autonomous commissioning and extensive documentation. Explainability requires transparent feasibility assessments, reasoning traces, environmental influence reporting, multimodal explanations and comprehensive logging. Evaluation should span diverse benchmarks, worst‑case distribution‑shift tests, fault‑tolerance, generalisation and metrics covering accuracy, safety, robustness, energy and compliance. Data efficiency emphasises few‑shot/zero‑shot adaptation, modality‑agnostic learning without retraining, self‑assessment for gap detection, and adherence to privacy and legal constraints.
